title: Why trees shed their leaves for winter
description: Broad leaves are a liability in winter — trees cut their losses, reclaim the nutrients and drop them before the cold arrives.

body.heading: Leaves are summer equipment
paragraphs: A broad, thin leaf is a superb solar panel, but it is also fragile and thirsty: it loses water constantly and is easily killed by frost. In winter, when soil water may be frozen and storms batter bare branches, keeping leaves would cost a tree more than they earn.
So deciduous trees — oaks, maples, birches — treat leaves as disposable summer equipment. As days shorten in autumn, the tree begins an orderly shutdown, recovering what it can before letting go.

body.heading: Salvage first, then cut
paragraphs: The tree first withdraws valuable nutrients from each leaf, including the green pigment chlorophyll. As the green fades, yellow and orange pigments that were there all along are unmasked — autumn colour is partly a salvage operation revealed.

Then a layer of corky cells, the abscission layer, forms across the base of the leaf stalk, weakening it and sealing the tree's side against water loss and infection. A gust of wind finishes the job, and the leaf falls, leaving a sealed scar.

body.heading: Nothing wasted
paragraphs: The fallen leaves are not litter but a resource: they insulate the soil, shelter insects and worms, and rot down into food for the tree's own roots — a slow refund of minerals. Gardeners who rake every leaf away are exporting the tree's savings.

Evergreens play the opposite strategy. Pines and hollies keep narrow, waxy, tough leaves that sip water and shrug off frost, ready to photosynthesise on any mild winter day — slower, steadier, and in no need of an annual rebuild. Their leaves are pre-fitted for the slow lane too: built to last several years, then dropped a few at a time rather than all at once.

takeaway: Deciduous trees shed leaves to survive winter's cold and drought, first reclaiming nutrients, then sealing off each leaf with a corky abscission layer.
